title: Not with a Bang but a Whimper: Congressional Silence Amid an Historic Assault on the Power of the Purse
one_line: A seven-page analysis essay (PS 59:456-462) arguing that Congress offered little resistance to unprecedented presidential impoundments and unilateral tariffs, and attributing the silence to partisan incentives and the president's dominance of his own party.
key_claims: The abstract makes four distinct claims needing different evidence: that the scope and breadth of the unilateral actions is a departure; that there were clear statutory violations; that there was widespread public opposition; and that Congress nonetheless offered little resistance, a stark departure from historical precedent.

The constitutional baseline is Article I Section 9 (no money drawn but by appropriation) and Article I Section 8 (duties and imposts), with tariff authority delegated to the president across a century of statutes mostly conditioned on national-security or emergency findings — so the claim is about the scope of exercise, not the novelty of delegation.

The Impoundment Control Act of 1974, written by the Congress that had just experienced Nixon's impoundments, sets a rescission procedure: Congress has 45 days of continuous session to agree, and absent agreement the money must be obligated — which is why the episode is framed as unprecedented.

The durable structural point is that the 1974 Act has no self-executing enforcement: the remedy is political plus whatever courts decide, so a Congress unwilling to defend its own appropriations leaves the statute toothless regardless of who holds the office.

The proposed mechanism is partisan incentives plus presidential dominance of the party; the hosts note Episode 72's preregistered experiment supplies the micro-foundation this essay lacks but could borrow.
limitations: The load-bearing comparative claim has no counted baseline: no series of oversight hearings, obligation-compelling appropriations riders, termination-resolution floor votes, subpoenas or institutional lawsuits coded consistently across administrations, so 'stark departure' is a narrative comparison to Nixon rather than a measurement.

Unified government confounds the mechanism: partisan incentives and institutional erosion predict identical silence in this period, and the comparisons that would separate them (a same-party Congress facing a same-party president's impoundment, or an opposition Congress under the same statute) are unavailable.

Silence is an absence and the public record cannot adjudicate it — private bargaining and anticipated reaction both code as inaction, while cheap-talk letters inflate apparent resistance, which argues for counting only costly actions.

The case-study genre selects on the dependent variable — episodes where Congress stayed quiet — so no rate of congressional pushback can be estimated, though the claim is about two specific large episodes rather than a rate.
The 'widespread public opposition' premise is load-bearing but unaccompanied in the abstract by item wording or margins, and tariff and spending-cut polling is highly wording-sensitive.
The statutory-violation claim is a legal judgment resting on institutional authorities rather than political-science measurement, and the hosts could not identify which authorities are relied on.
The paper is paywalled: the hosts worked from the abstract and surrounding literature and said so, and the article went to press before the relevant litigation resolved.
open_questions: Build a counted series of hearings, riders and termination votes per Congress across four or five administrations with published coding rules, and show recent Congresses sitting below that distribution.
Pre-commit to a numerical threshold — defections or enacted riders — that would have counted as resistance, as Episode 82 did with its falsification bar.
Watch the next appropriations cycle for hard obligation language and reporting deadlines, which would mean Congress defended itself slowly rather than not at all.
Find or construct a case that separates partisan incentives from institutional erosion outside unified government.
